Why is so much called “black magic” these days? In acoustics, hi-fi and NVH (noise, vibration and harshness) are the two fields that most often get the label. What they have in common is that both involve human perception, and so, as the Tao Te Ching puts it, they are “mystery upon mystery, the gateway to all wonders.” I don’t know much about hi-fi; I can’t even recognize its most basic Chinese jargon, so I won’t presume to comment. As I see it, NVH is black magic partly because of the human factor and partly because a car is an extremely complex structure, which makes its acoustic behavior complex too.

A car is a complex structure

As every acoustician knows, any sound problem has three elements: the source, the transmission path and the receiver.

In a car, the familiar main sources are engine noise, wind noise and tire/road noise, and plenty of people on Zhihu have explained those already.

I want to talk about some of the odds and ends that make noise inside a car. They fit the black-magic theme rather better.

HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning)

HVAC components are spread all over the cabin, and premium cars have even more of them. Turn the fan up high and the noise inevitably goes up with it. Take one BMW model: a scan with the Scan&Paint 3D system showed that the main noise energy of the HVAC system was concentrated at 100–500 Hz and 980–1,300 Hz.

Steering-column stalks

Yes, people really do work on the acoustics of these. Now that manufacturing has passed its peak, comfort is getting more attention than ever before. Again, this is especially true of premium brands. Carmakers that once cared only about sound pressure level are increasingly looking at psychoacoustic metrics such as sharpness and roughness, so suppliers at every tier have to keep pace, and acoustic research is in full swing.

Below is a spectrogram of one stalk, showing how flicking it differs from letting it go. Both events are close to impulses, so they are broadband. The flick is short; the release lasts longer, because the stalk swings back and forth a few times before it settles.

The next images show where the sound comes from when the stalk is flicked and when it is released, measured with Microflown’s acoustic camera.

Once the sources are located, the supplier can dig deeper into the psychoacoustic metrics and work out manufacturing measures to improve the product. This is where the black magic comes in. Staying within the specified ranges for the psychoacoustic metrics is one thing. Improving the sound quality, making a part sound premium and refined, or simply more beautiful, is much harder.

The fragrance dispenser

WTF???

That was my first reaction too. Some cars really do have one, and it isn’t filled with any ordinary scent, but with one that “smells like a new car.”

It usually sits in the glovebox in front of the passenger seat, with a small motor inside that spreads the scent.

Don’t underestimate it. When the cabin is quiet, it is close enough to the driver to be heard, and since the motor noise is mostly pure tones, it is pretty annoying.

The audio system

This one isn’t noise, strictly speaking. I’m just padding the list.

When you lay out a car audio system, you want the sound field at the left and right ears to be balanced, not only in level but also in frequency response. That is what makes the sound immersive and pleasing to the ear. You also want to keep cabin modes away from the driver’s head.

There are plenty more: the gear lever, window actuators, doors opening and closing, the reversing beeper and so on. I won’t go through them all.

Human perception

As I said at the start, this is where the black magic really comes from.

When I sat in on the Sound Engineering course taught by Professor Klaus Genuit of HEAD acoustics, one slide made a deep impression on me.

Who knew that preferences in car sound could differ so much from country to country? Of course, not everyone fits the pattern, but these are the averages. Tune a car’s acoustics in that direction for each market and it will sell better.

But what is “sporty”? What is “aggressive”? What is “powerful”? Again, the answer is an average that takes a lot of statistics to pin down. Each major carmaker probably has its own recipe: which frequency bands make a car sound sporty, how the levels should be balanced, and so on. That recipe is then mapped onto individual components, and the various departments and suppliers at every tier work out together how to tune them. I don’t know the specific measures well enough to go any deeper.

A car is a complex structure, with tens of thousands of parts working together, and all their combinations throw up acoustic problems without end. Each supplier tests the acoustic behavior of its parts, then thumps its chest and tells the carmaker everything’s fine. The carmaker puts the part in a car, tests it and fires back: “Bullshit, this is nothing like what you told us.” The supplier takes the part back and goes to have it out with its own supplier. And that’s all based on objective measurements. Add subjective perception, and an already complex problem becomes even more complex. So calling NVH black magic is fair enough.

Then again, if it weren’t black magic, what would keep acoustic engineers in work? Now electric vehicles are bearing down on us with a whole new set of acoustic problems. So bring it on, and aim straight for our most sensitive spots!
